title: Do you have to leave?
hookLine: the prince left home; most Buddhists never have. An old couple asks the Buddha how to stay together, in this life and the next (AN 4.55)

lines: AN EMPTY ROOM AT THE PALACE.
cards: On the riverbank, the prince sends Channa home with the white horse. In the later telling, Kanthaka's heart breaks on the road, and he dies of grief. Back at the palace, a wife and a newborn son wake up to an empty room.
It's the part of the story many people find hardest. And it raises a question a lot of newcomers carry quietly: if this is the path, do I have to leave the people I love?
Today, the answer the old texts give, through a married couple.

teach.b: Start with who was there. The early texts describe the Buddha's community as four groups: monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen. The lay followers are called upasaka and upasika.
They farmed, traded, married, raised children, and most Buddhists in history have lived that way. Now the couple.
In a town called Sumsumaragira lived an old householder known as Nakula's father, and his wife, Nakula's mother.

One day he tells the Buddha: since she was brought to my home as a young girl, I don't remember being unfaithful to her, not even in thought. We want to see each other in this life, and in the next one too.
She says the same. The Buddha doesn't tell them to let each other go.

teach.h: NAKULA'S PARENTS: TOGETHER, THIS LIFE AND NEXT.
teach.b: He tells them how: if a husband and wife both wish to stay together, in this life and the next, let them be matched in four things, faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom.
Later he named the two of them foremost among his lay followers in trust. So what is the letting go that the teaching asks for?

teach.h: LET GO OF THE GRIP, NOT THE LOVE.
teach.b: Teachers draw a line between love and the grip.
Love wishes someone well. The grip needs them never to change, never to leave, never to be anything but yours. That grip is where so much fear lives, and that's what the practice loosens.
Monks and nuns choose a different life, and the tradition honors them. But for most people on this path, the practice happens at a kitchen table, with the people they love.

how: Most Buddhists are lay followers who practice at home, keeping the five precepts, giving, and visiting the temple on holy days, while monks and nuns live the renunciant life the prince chose.

o: a temple helper who cooks for the monks
a lay follower who practices at home
a novice monk in his first year of training

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: a lay follower who practices at home
an old couple who hoped to meet again
the horse sent home without him

s: to practice, you have to leave your family
most Buddhists in history were householders; laymen and laywomen are part of the community.
the Buddha told a married couple how to stay together across lives
be matched in faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom.
what's let go is the grip, the need to own and freeze someone, not the love.

games.q: you're an old householder. you tell the Buddha you've been faithful to your wife since she was a girl, and you want to be together in the next life too. what does he say?
o: let her go; attachment binds you.
be matched in faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom.
become a monk, and you'll meet again.
games.why: he doesn't tell them to let each other go. he tells them how to stay together: four qualities, shared.

practice: Bring to mind someone you love, see their face, and let the warmth that comes with it stay. Notice whether there's a tightness somewhere under the warmth, a worry, a need for them to stay just as they are, and don't push it away.
Just breathe out a little longer, and see if the tightness softens while the warmth stays.

wordCard.voice: Upasaka. A lay follower, one who sits close: the person who practices at home, with family and work. Upasika for a woman. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: a lay follower, literally one who sits close or attends; a laywoman is upasika, उपासिका.

carryVoice: Your line: love without the grip. What the path loosens is the clutching, never the love. Day forty.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 4.55 (Samajivi Sutta): Nakula's parents wish to meet in the next life
